General Goals:Awareness of chronic non-communicable diseases – prevalence and health implications Introducing the concept of metabolic diseases and nutritional pathology: diabetes mellitus, obesity, metabolic syndrome, dyslipidemia, hyperuricemia, healthy nutrition. NCDs #11

  • Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) – cancer, cardiovascular disease, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes – are the #1 cause of death and disability worldwide, accounting for
  •  74% of all deaths
  • Every two seconds, a person dies prematurely from an NCD
  • 85% of premature deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries.
  • more than three out of four years lived with a disability
  • More 41 millions of death / year

NCDs #12

  • NCDs are a relatively new priority on the global health agenda, with the first UN High-Level Meetings on NCDs taking place in 2011 and 2014.
  • These focused on a ‘4x4’ approach; that is, four main NCDs – cardiovascular diseases (CVD), cancer, diabetes, and chronic respiratory diseases – and four main modifiable risk factors – tobacco and alcohol use, unhealthy diet, and physical inactivity.
  • https://ncdalliance.org/

Slide 13 #13

  • In 2018, the third UN High-Level Meeting on NCDs also formally recognised mental health and air pollution as core components of the NCD response
  • thereby introducing the ‘5x5’ approach.
  • While the top five diseases make up the largest burden of morbidity and mortality from NCDs, there are hundreds of other important diseases and conditions that also need addressing outside the 5x5 to tackle NCDs.

5x5 Diseases #14

  • Cancer is a leading cause of chronic-disease related death in the world, with around 10 million people dying from cancer every year. While the global burden of cancer is increasing, at least one-third of cancers are preventable, and many cases and deaths can be averted through prevention and early detection.
  • Cardiovascular disease (CVD) - including heart attacks and stroke - kills more people globally than any other disease, accounting for nearly 18 million deaths per year with around one-third of these deaths occurring before 70 years of age.
  • Diabetes is one of the world’s most common diseases, and is a leading cause of death. As diabetes rates increase year-on-year, access to treatment and care is a major global health challenge, with about 50% of people living with diabetes unable to access a regular supply of the insulin they need to survive.
  • Chronic respiratory diseases, including asthma, are under-recognised, under-diagnosed, under-treated & insufficiently prevented.
  • Mental health is a state of wellbeing where people and societies function at their best.

Conditions outside the 5x5 #15

  • Eye health conditions include refractive error, cataracts, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration and other diseases that affect our vision.
  • Oral health diseases including tooth decay, tooth loss, and periodontal disease affect around 3.5 billion people globally, almost half of the world’s population. In fact, they are the most common NCD.
  • Obesity is a known risk-factor for many NCDs but is also increasingly considered a disease in its own right. NCD deaths attributable to obesity have risen to 5 million per year while effective actions to both prevent and treat obesity remains stagnant.
  • Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is increasingly recognised as a global health priority.
  • Thyroid conditions can lead to serious health issues if not treated,

Risk factors #22

  • Modifiable behavioural risk factors
  • - Tobacco accounts for around 7.2 million deaths every year (including from the effects of exposure to second-hand smoke), and is projected to increase to 8 million by 2030.
  • - About 3.2 million deaths annually can be attributed to insufficient physical activity.
  • - More than half of the 3.3 million annual deaths from harmful drinking
  • - 4.1 million annual deaths have been attributed to excess salt/sodium intake
  • Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs)

Risk factors #23

  • Metabolic/physiological risk factors
  • - These behaviours lead to four key metabolic/physiological changes that increase the risk of NCDs:
  • - raised blood pressure,
  • - overweight/obesity,
  • - hyperglycemia (high blood glucose levels) and
  • - hyperlipidemia (high levels of fat in the blood).
  • In terms of attributable deaths, the leading metabolic risk factor globally is elevated blood pressure (to which 18% of global deaths are attributed) followed by overweight and obesity and raised blood glucose.
  • Low- and middle-income countries are witnessing the fastest rise in overweight young children.
  • Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs)

NCDs Key facts #24

  • Cancer is a leading cause of chronic-disease related death in the world, with around 10 million people dying from cancer every year. While the global burden of cancer is increasing, at , and many cases and deaths can be averted through prevention and early detection.
  • Cardiovascular disease (CVD) - including heart attacks and stroke - kills more people globally than any other disease, accounting for nearly 18 million deaths per year with around one-third of these deaths occurring before 70 years of age..

NCDs Key facts #25

  • Diabetes is one of the world’s most common diseases, and is a leading cause of death. As diabetes rates increase year-on-year, access to treatment and care is a major global health challenge, with about 50% of people living with diabetes unable to access a regular supply of the insulin they need to survive.
  • Chronic respiratory diseases, including asthma, are under-recognised, under-diagnosed, under-treated & insufficiently prevented. Although breath is fundamental to life, lung health is less well recognised as a critical health factor than other indicators, such as weight and blood pressure.

Key facts - Non-Communicable Diseases #26

  • NCDs will cost the world economy $47 trillion over the next 20 years, representing 75 % of global GDP (Gross domestic product) and surpassing the cost of the global financial crisis
  • WHO 2011

NCD #27

  • Are largely preventable by means of effective interventions that tackle shared risk factors, namely: tobacco use, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity and harmful use of alcohol.
  • If the major risk factors for chronic disease were eliminated, at around 75 % of heart disease, stroke and type 2 diabetes and 40% of cancer would be prevented

Prevention and control of NCDs #28

  • - a comprehensive approach that requires all sectors, including health, finance, foreign affairs, education, agriculture, planning and others, to work together to reduce the risks associated with NCDs, as well as promote the interventions to prevent and control them.
  • to focus on the risk factors : tobacco use, unhealthy diet and physical inactivity, and the harmful use of alcohol
  • primary health-care approach to strengthen early detection and timely treatment.

Slide 29 #29

Metabolic diseases and COVID-19 #30

  • WHO: mortality rate of patients with COVID-19 and other comorbidities:
  • 13.2% in the case of cardiovascular diseases,
  • 9.2% in the case of DM
  • 8.4% in case of hypertension,
  • 90.5% of deaths - at least one comorbidity, 30.1% had diabetes
  • The presence of diabetes was 3 x higher in those with severe evolution of COVID-19 infection and in a proportion of 31% in those who died.
  • The risk of death is 3-7 times higher in people with previously uncontrolled diabetes and especially during COVD-19 infection.

Metabolic diseases and COVID-19 #31

  • The average survival time from hospitalization was shorter in those with diabetes and severe forms of COVID-19, respectively 10 days, compared to 18 days in those without diabetes.
  • Patients with DM and COVID-19 have more severe forms of pneumonia, organ damage, inflammatory factors and hypercoalgulability, with progression to a poor prognosis.
  • Previous diabetes and hyperglycemia during hospitalization for COVID-19 - 29% mortality rate - 4 x higher than in those without diabetes and with normoglycemia.
  • Hyperglycemias during hospitalization - 42% deaths - mortality rate 7 x higher compared to those without diabetes and normoglycemias.

COVID-19 and risk of diabetes #32

  • Increased risk for diabetes among persons aged <18 years with COVID-19
  • People who get COVID-19 have a greater risk of developing diabetes up to a year later = 40 %, even after a mild SARS-CoV-2 infection, compared with those who never had the disease, a massive study of almost 200,000 people shows.

Metabolic diseases and COVID-19 #33

  • Obesity has been highlighted as a risk factor for severe COVID-19
  • The risk of severe COVID-19 was markedly increased in the severely obese group (body mass index > 35) – 7 times
  • Obesity was a risk factor for both admission to intensive care and mortality from COVID-19
  • Cardiovascular diseases are associated with increased risks for severe COVID-19 and mortality.
  • Risk factors for NCDs can make people more vulnerable to becoming severely ill with COVID-19
  • People with NCDs are “among the most likely to become severely ill and die” from COVID-19

Chronic Metabolic diseases in general population (CMD) #34

  • Diabetes mellitus, obesity, dyslipidemia and the metabolic syndrome are defined as chronic metabolic diseases (CMD) with a high prevalence in general population, representing a major health problem, in both developed and developing countries.
  • CMD - highest impact on population health.
  • - represented 46% of the whole world pathology in 2001,
  • - accounting for 60% global mortality.

Metabolic diseases- Impact #35

  • 2. Epidemiologic impact : very high prevalence
  • obesity epidemic
  • pre-diabetes- & diabetes epidemic

  • 3. Economic, social impact:
  • increased cost of medical services

  • CMD have a triple impact: individual, epidemiological and socio-economic.
  • Individual impact involves:
  • dramatic decrease of life expectancy
  • decrease/ alteration of quality of life

  • -way of living of individuals, families and societies, which they manifest in coping with their physical, psychological, social, and economic environments on a day-to-day basis.
  • Lifestyle is expressed in both work and leisure behavior patterns and (on an individual basis) in activities, attitudes, interests, opinions, values, and allocation of income.
  • -It also reflects people's self image or self concept; the way they see themselves and believe they are seen by the others.
  • -Lifestyle is a composite of motivations, needs, and desires and is influenced by factors such as culture, family, reference groups, and social class.

Slide 51 #51

  • DM is a metabolic chronic disease of multiple aetiology characterized by chronic hyperglycaemia with disturbances of carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism resulting from defects of insulin secretion, insulin action, or a combination of
  • both.
  • DM is associated with development of specific long-term organ damage (diabetes complications) including retinopathy with potential blindness, nephropathy with a risk of progression to renal failure, neuropathy with risk for foot ulcers, amputation, autonomic dysfunction such as sexual impairment.
  • Patients with diabetes are at a particularly high risk for cardiovascular,cerebrovascular, and peripheral artery disease.
  • Associated with: - reduced life expectancy, quality of life.

  • type 1 diabetes (results from -cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency) accounts for only 5–10% of those with diabetes, has multifactorial aetiology. There are 2 subtypes: autoimmune and idiopatic.

Gestational diabetes mellitus #69

  • (GDM)
  • any glycemic abnormality diagnosed during pregnancy

Pregnancy and Hyperglycemia #70

  • Major effect of chronic hyperglycemia:
  • - During the 1st trimester of pregnancy- hyperglycemia (>150 mg/dl) -3-fold increased risk of foetal abnormalities and 4-8-fold increased risk of spontaneous abortion
  • - macrosomia – 7-fold more frequent
  • FPG above 90 - 95 mg/dl compared with 75 mg/dl,
  • macrosomia – 14-fold increased risk
  • FPG  105 mg/dl.
  • Congenital malformations - 25 % in uncontrolled (HbA1c>10%) pre-gestational DM (type 1 or type 2)
  • G. Roman, N. Costin. Diabetes and Pregnancy-Îndrumar de practică medicală. 2005

Perinatal Mortality in GDM #71

  • - 2.6% (OR 2.3) în untreated GDM
  • - Postprandial hyperglycemia< 140 mg/dl – 75% reduction of PNM.
  • Perinatal mortality in pre-existing DM
  • - glycemic average= 100 mg/dl PNM – 4 %
  • - glycemic average = 100–150 mg/dl PNM – 15 %
  • - glycemic average = >150 mg/dl PNM – 24 %
  • Continuous increase of PNM for glycemic values > 100 mg/dl
  • Pregnancy and hyperglycemia
  • Moshe Hod M., Yogev Y. Goals of Metabolic Management of Gestational Diabetes. Diabetes Care, 2007, 30

GDM screening – increased risk subjects #72

  • Overweight or obesity (BMI> 25 kg/m2) pre-pregnancy
  • Excessive weight gain during the first 6 months of pregnancy
  • Mother older age (over 35 years)
  • Multiparity
  • History of IFG or IGT
  • Members of ethnic populations at high risk for GDM
  • Prior history of GDM or delivery of large-for-gestational-age infant
  • Excessive weight gain
  • History of macrosomia or foetal hypotrophy
  • History of foetal mortality
  • Diagnosis of PCOS
  • Strong family history of type 2 diabetes

Screening GDM #73

  • Women at high risk should be screened for diabetes as soon as possible after the confirmation of pregnancy (before week 24) at the first prenatal visit
  • If result is negative, repeat test in week 24-28;
  • Women at moderate risk should be screened in week 24-28.

Type 1 DM - Epidemiology #87

  • Type 1 diabetes is a disease of insulin deficiency and accounts for 5–10% of all cases of diabetes.
  • It typically presents in childhood and young adulthood, reaching a peak incidence around the time of puberty, but can present at any age.
  • Type 1 diabetes is subdivided into type 1A (immune- mediated)
  • and type 1B (non- immune- mediated). The vast majority have type 1A disease.
  • A variant with slower progression to insulin deficiency occurs in later life and is termed latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA).

Type 1 DM - Pathogenesis #88

  • Autoimmune disease – multifactorial aetiology- interaction between genetic and environmental factors
  • Immune reaction against pancreatic β-cells
  • Markers of the immune destruction of the β-cell include:
  • islet cell autoantibodies (ICA),
  • autoantibodies to insulin (IAA),
  • autoantibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65),
  • autoantibodies to the tyrosine phosphatases IA-2 and IA-2β.
  • Zinc Transporter 8 antibodies (ZnT8)

T1 DM – Aetiology #92

  • Type 1 diabetes belongs to a family of immune-mediated organ-specific diseases, which include autoimmune thyroid disease, coeliac disease, Addison’s disease and pernicious anaemia.
  • The precise molecular mechanisms that lead to T1DM are incompletely understood but involve the triggering of a selective autoimmune destruction of the insulin producing cells of a genetically predisposed individual.
  • Initially, autoantibodies directed against pancreatic islet constituents appear in the circulation and often predate clinical onset by many years.

T1 DM – Aetiology #93

  • The islet antigens include insulin itself, the enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), protein tyrosine phosphatase (IA-2, also known as ICA512), the cation transporter ZnT8 and
  • This is followed by a phase of asymptomatic loss of β cell
  • secretory capacity; histologically, this is characterized by a chronic inflammatory mononuclear cell infiltrate of T lymphocytes and macrophages in the islets, known as insulitis
  • Eventually, when the remaining β cells are no longer able to produce enough insulin to meet the body’s needs, diabetes symptoms start to develop.

T1 DM – Aetiology #94

  • Some recovery of endogenous insulin secretion may occur over the first few months after diagnosis and treatment initiation (the ‘honeymoon period’).
  • During this time, the insulin dose may need to be reduced or even stopped.

Type 2 diabetes mellitus – Epidemiology #95

  • Type 2 diabetes is the most common form of diabetes, accounting for around 90% of all cases; it is also one of the most common non-communicable diseases.
  • The prevalence of type 2 diabetes is rising rapidly because of a combination of population growth, an ageing population (Pancreatic β-cell function declines with age ) and longer survival with type 2 diabetes, earlier age at onset and better diagnosis.
  • Type 2 diabetes is a disease of nutrient excess and the incidence has increased with the obesity epidemic, poor quality diet and reduced physical activity.

Obesity #96

  • Obesity increases the risk of T2DM up to 80–100-fold and accounts for 80–85% of the overall risk of developing T2DM.
  • 80–90% of adults with T2DM are overweight and nearly a half are obese.
  • A central distribution of fat increases the risk of T2DM , and so for any given level of obesity, the more visceral fat an individual has, the higher the risk of T2DM.
  • Risk factors

Diet #97

  • Although diet can affect the risk of diabetes through changes in body weight, certain dietary patterns are associated with higher or lower risks of type 2 diabetes.
  • Components that increase the risk include:
  • dietary fat, particularly saturated fat, red and processed meat, consumption of fried food, including French fries, increased intake of white rice and sugar-sweetened beverages.
  • Wholegrains, increased fruit and vegetable intake, fermented dairy products, oily fish and a Mediterranean dietary pattern are associated with lower rates of type 2 diabetes.
  • Risk factors

Physical inactivity #98

  • Physical inactivity and sedentary behaviour are also associated with an increased risk of diabetes.
  • Other factors
  • Other risk factors include urbanization, poverty, abnormal sleep patterns,
  • environmental toxins and mental illness.
